issues.legal_issue: A permanent exemption of buildings based solely on their construction after a cutoff date violates equality when the original incentive for construction no longer rationally justifies the continuing difference in treatment.
material_facts: The exemption applied indefinitely to buildings constructed after a specified cutoff, while older buildings were subject to rent control.
Many exempt buildings had become old, and their landlords had received rental income for many years and recovered a substantial part of their investment.
The exemption created different treatment for landlords and tenants depending on the construction date of the building.
The original purpose of the exemption was to encourage building activity, but the State did not show how exempting buildings constructed many years earlier continued to encourage new construction.
issues.conclusion: The permanent construction-date exemption was unconstitutional under Article 14 and was quashed.
issues.legal_principle: Article 14 permits classification only when it rests on an intelligible differentia and that differentia has a rational relation to the statute’s object. Applying Shri Ram Krishna Dalmia v. Shri Justice S.R. Tendolkar, the Court held that the construction-date classification no longer had that relationship once the incentive rationale ceased to justify the continuing exemption. The Court also relied on State of Madhya Pradesh v. Bhopal Sugar Industries Ltd., Vishwesha Thirtha Swamiar v. State of Mysore, H.H. Shri Swamiji of Shri Admar Mutt v. Commissioner, Hindu Religious & Charitable Endowments Department, and Narottam Kishore Dev Varma v. Union of India for the principle that a measure initially justified may become discriminatory as circumstances change. Chintapalli Achaiah v. P. Gopalakrishna Reddy was overruled.

rule.if: constitutional_challenge_to_building_exemption and permanent_construction_date_exemption and unequal_treatment_by_building_age and (exempt_buildings_have_aged or construction_incentive_no_longer_justifies_exemption)

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_building_exe: A party brought a constitutional challenge to a statutory exemption from rent-control rules for a category of buildings.
predicates.permanent_construction_date_exemption: The exemption applied indefinitely to buildings classified by when they were constructed.
predicates.unequal_treatment_by_building_age: The classification subjected landlords or tenants to different legal treatment based on the age or construction date of a building.
predicates.exempt_buildings_have_aged: Buildings that remained exempt had become old, and their owners had had time to recover a substantial part of their investment through rents.
predicates.construction_incentive_no_longer_justifi: The original incentive for constructing buildings no longer rationally explained why those already-built buildings should remain exempt.

issues.definition: When a constitutional challenge concerns a permanent exemption based on construction date, and that classification creates unequal treatment after exempt buildings have aged or the construction incentive no longer justifies the exemption, the exemption is unconstitutional.

issues.legal_issue: A provision that was constitutionally justified when enacted may later become discriminatory when its justification disappears, and its earlier approval or continued existence does not prevent a later constitutional challenge.
material_facts: The exemption had previously been upheld by a High Court on the view that the hardship to tenants would be temporary.
The exemption continued for more than two decades without a time limit.
The original justification was to encourage new building activity, but the continuing exemption for already-built buildings no longer served that purpose.
The petitioners relied on the continued and unjustified unequal treatment to challenge the provision.
issues.conclusion: The provision could be challenged and struck down after its original justification had ceased; neither its earlier approval nor the passage of time made it constitutional.
issues.legal_principle: Article 14 may be violated when a measure that was initially justified becomes discriminatory as circumstances change. The Court relied on the reasoning in Bhaiyalal Shukla v. State of Madhya Pradesh, State of Madhya Pradesh v. Bhopal Sugar Industries Ltd., Vishwesha Thirtha Swamiar v. State of Mysore, H.H. Shri Swamiji of Shri Admar Mutt v. Commissioner, Hindu Religious & Charitable Endowments Department, and Narottam Kishore Dev Varma v. Union of India. It held that lapse of time does not confer constitutionality on an otherwise unconstitutional provision.

rule.if: constitutional_challenge_to_existing_law and initially_justified_classification and original_justification_has_ceased and continued_unequal_treatment

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_existing_law: A party brought a constitutional challenge to a law that remained in force.
predicates.initially_justified_classification: The classification had a rational justification when the law was introduced.
predicates.original_justification_has_ceased: Changed circumstances meant that the original rationale no longer supported the classification.
predicates.continued_unequal_treatment: The law continued to treat similarly situated people differently after its original rationale had ceased.

issues.definition: If an existing law continues to impose unequal treatment after the justification that initially supported its classification has ceased, it may be struck down despite having been previously upheld or remaining in force.

issues.legal_issue: Invalidating a severable exemption does not invalidate the remainder of a rent-control statute when the remaining provisions are workable and consistent with legislative intent.
material_facts: The challenged clause was an exception to the wider rent-control law.
The remaining provisions could operate without the exception.
The law replaced earlier rent-control laws that had protected tenants in the constituent areas.
The Court concluded that the legislature would still have enacted the rent-control law without the challenged exception.
issues.conclusion: The exemption was severable, and the remainder of the Act remained in force and applied to buildings regardless of their construction date, subject to other valid exemptions.
issues.legal_principle: Under the doctrine of severability, an unconstitutional provision may be removed while the rest of a statute remains valid if the remaining provisions are complete and workable and the legislature would have enacted them independently. The Court relied on Dorchy v. Kansas, Cooley’s Constitutional Limitations, R.M.D. Chamarbaugwalla v. Union of India, and D.S. Nakara v. Union of India.

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_statutory_ex: A party challenged the constitutionality of an exception contained in a broader statutory scheme.
predicates.exception_is_unconstitutional: The challenged exception was found to violate constitutional requirements.
predicates.remaining_law_is_workable_without_except: The other provisions can operate as a complete and workable law after the exception is removed.
predicates.legislature_would_have_enacted_remaining: The history and purpose of the legislation show that the legislature intended the remaining law to operate without the invalid exception.

issues.definition: If an unconstitutional exception can be removed while the rest of the law remains workable and accords with legislative intent, the remaining law stays in force.

issues.legal_issue: Invalidating the exemption does not disturb an eviction decree that has become final when the landlord has already taken possession under it.
material_facts: The Court expressly limited the effect of its declaration of invalidity for eviction proceedings in which a civil court’s decree had become final.
The limitation applied where the landlord had already taken possession of the building under that decree.
issues.conclusion: The declaration of invalidity did not affect a final eviction decree where the landlord had already taken possession pursuant to it.
issues.legal_principle: The Court expressly preserved the validity of completed eviction proceedings in which the decree had become final and possession had already been taken. The judgment does not cite an earlier case or a separate statutory provision for this limitation.

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_building_exe: A party brought a constitutional challenge to a statutory exemption from rent-control rules for a category of buildings.
predicates.final_eviction_decree_exists: An eviction decree had become final in the relevant proceeding.
predicates.landlord_already_has_possession: The landlord had already taken possession under the final decree.

issues.definition: When a constitutional challenge to a building exemption is decided after an eviction decree has become final and the landlord has taken possession under it, the completed eviction proceeding is not affected.
